tagline.text: A financial city hiding museums and weekend markets among its skyscrapers

items.credit: Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: The center of Philippine finance and business, where Ayala Avenue's high-rises, big shopping malls, and hotels cluster together. From the Ayala Museum and Ayala Triangle Gardens to weekend morning markets and the lanes of Poblacion that come alive at night, you can enjoy Manila's modern face in a single day.

Makati sits in the heart of Metro Manila, south of the Pasig River, and serves as the country's center of finance, commerce, and diplomacy. Banks, multinational headquarters, embassies, and upscale hotels line Ayala Avenue, Paseo de Roxas, and Buendia Avenue in dense clusters. Its resident population is only about 300,000, but millions pass through each day for work and shopping.
Its history runs longer than you might expect. It was founded as the town of "San Pedro de Macati" in the Spanish era around
, and today's Poblacion still holds the Church of San Pedro and San Pablo, completed around
. In

, the Zobel de Ayala family bought up farmland in the area, and before World War II the district was home to Nielson Field, one of Manila's early airports. After the war, the Ayala family laid out roads and buildings in a planned scheme over the old runways, and today's central business district took shape from the
onward. The two long roads where Ayala Avenue and Paseo de Roxas cross are traces of that former runway.
Makati has also been a stage for modern Philippine history — as in the scene of yellow confetti pouring from buildings along Ayala Avenue during the

People Power Revolution. Today, travelers know it more for shopping, dining, and nightlife. Its network of walkable footbridges and connected parks, along with security that's relatively good by Manila standards, also makes it a comfortable base for first-time visitors to Manila.

It's not a city packed with sightseeing landmarks, but between the Ayala Museum, which lays out Philippine history in one place, weekend morning food markets, and countless restaurants and rooftop bars, it's easy to fill a day well. It suits families, business travelers, and anyone who loves shopping and good food, and pairing it with neighboring BGC or Manila's old town rounds out a richer city trip.

Known for an exhibit that walks through Philippine history using 60 handcrafted dioramas, and for "Gold of Ancestors," a collection of more than 1,000 pieces of pre-colonial gold jewelry. It sits inside Greenbelt, so it's easy to combine with shopping.
A roughly two-hectare green park in the middle of the skyscrapers, where the old control tower building of Nielson Airport survives as a restaurant. From
November to January
, an evening light-and-music show is held here nightly.
Food markets run on Saturdays at Jaime Velasquez Park in Salcedo Village, and on Sundays at Legazpi Active Park in Legazpi Village. They typically run from
7 AM to 2 PM
, offering everything from Filipino home cooking to international dishes, organic produce, and handicrafts in one place.

Ayala Center — Greenbelt with its gardens, the huge Glorietta mall, One Ayala, and Landmark, all linked by covered walkways — is the heart of Makati shopping. Greenbelt 1 is under redevelopment, so check which stores are currently open.

Once old downtown Makati, Poblacion's narrow lanes have become a nightlife strip packed with craft-beer pubs, rooftop bars, and restaurants from around the world. It's liveliest from dusk until midnight.

children.text: A Spanish-era church on a hill in Poblacion, a trace of the days when Makati was a small riverside town. It offers a quiet atmosphere completely different from the skyscrapers nearby.
Rooftop bars atop Makati's hotels and office towers look out over the lit-up Ayala Avenue and BGC skylines, and even Manila Bay in the distance. A single cocktail runs about

Chino Roces Avenue's Little Tokyo is an old cluster of alleys full of Japanese restaurants, and Korean and other international restaurants are scattered throughout Makati. There's plenty of fun in choosing between Filipino food and dishes from around the world.

Ayala station on MRT-3, running along EDSA, connects directly to central Makati, and you can walk from the station to One Ayala and Glorietta. Buendia and Guadalupe stations are also in Makati. The fare is about

From Manila's old town, take LRT-1 and get off at EDSA station, then transfer to MRT-3 at Taft Avenue station. Trains are very crowded during rush hour, so if you're carrying a lot of luggage, take a Grab instead.
The EDSA Carousel bus, running in the dedicated center lane of EDSA, stops at the Ayala station. The fare is about
. From Clark International Airport, a P2P bus to Manila takes about
2–3 hours
— check current routes and stops.

Within the central business district, covered walkways and underpasses connect Ayala Center, Ayala Triangle, and Salcedo and Legazpi Villages. Jaywalking on the main roads is enforced, so always use a footbridge or underpass. It's about
20–25 minutes
on foot from Greenbelt to Poblacion; at night, a Grab is more convenient.
With its many malls and indoor spaces, Makati can be visited year-round, but the
December–April
dry season is best for walking and enjoying the outdoor markets.
December–February
mornings and evenings are relatively cool, while in
April–May
temperatures climb to
, making indoor plans more comfortable at midday.
During the
June–October

rainy season, afternoon showers and typhoons are frequent, and heavy rain can flood or badly jam roads around EDSA and Buendia. During the Christmas season, Ayala Avenue and the malls are decked out in elaborate decorations and Ayala Triangle hosts its light show, but traffic on Friday evenings and around paydays in
December
is the worst of the year. Schedule your travel for weekday daytime or weekend mornings whenever you can.

Makati offers the widest range of accommodation in Metro Manila. Around Ayala Center you'll find clusters of international chain luxury hotels (about
per night), while Legazpi and Salcedo Villages and the Buendia area have many serviced residences and business hotels (about
). Backpackers use the hostels in Poblacion (dorm beds about
), though these can stay noisy late into the night — choose somewhere in the central business district instead if you want quiet.

Food is at the heart of a Makati trip. Greenbelt and Ayala Triangle have many restaurants serving refined takes on Filipino cuisine, making it easy to try sinigang (a sour tamarind soup), kare-kare (a peanut-sauce stew), and lechon kawali (crispy fried pork belly). At the weekend markets, it's fun to sample a little of everything — grilled skewers, lechon, and the Filipino dessert halo-halo — while Poblacion gathers small restaurants from around the world, from tacos and ramen to Middle Eastern food. Chino Roces Avenue's Little Tokyo is an old alley of Japanese restaurants, and if you're missing Korean food, Korean restaurants and grocery stores are easy to find all over Makati.
Every mall and building entrance has a security check. It's routine to be asked to open your bag for a look, so don't be alarmed.
During rush hour (
7–9 AM
5–8 PM
), Grab fares rise and cars can be hard to find. Stick to sights within walking distance during these hours.
The Ayala Museum is often closed on Mondays. Check hours and admission on the
Ayala Museum official website
Cash is more convenient at the weekend markets. Some stalls accept e-wallets like GCash, but these can be hard for foreigners to use, so bring small bills.
Restaurant bills usually already include a 10% service charge. If it's included, there's no need to leave an additional tip.
Air conditioning inside the malls runs very cold. A light jacket is worth packing.
Currency exchange counters inside the malls tend to offer better rates than the airport. Compare rates at a few before you exchange.
In the nightlife strip around P. Burgos Street, overcharging, drink-spiking, and touts have been reported. Avoid drinks or venues pushed by strangers, and never leave your drink unattended.
Watch for pickpockets in crowded spots like Ayala MRT station and EDSA bus stops.
When hailing a taxi on the street, make sure the driver turns on the meter, and if they try to negotiate a flat fare, get out and take a Grab instead.
Rather than walking alone through Poblacion's lanes late at night, call a Grab from the main street.
Heavy rain floods low-lying roads quickly. Cut back on travel and check the latest updates if a typhoon warning is issued.
Avoid anyone who approaches offering to exchange currency, as well as street money changers — use a bank or a licensed exchange counter instead.
